outline.chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning in Large Language Models
outline.description: This chapter sets the stage by explaining why Reinforcement Learning (RL) is critical for advancing Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly in complex reasoning tasks. It introduces the fundamental challenge of training stability at scale, highlighting the risks of model collapse seen in current state-of-the-art methods like GRPO. The chapter concludes by introducing Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) as the proposed solution to these systemic instabilities.
subtopics: The role of RL in scaling LLM capabilities (reasoning, math, coding)
The crisis of training stability: Model collapse and irreversibility
Limitations of existing algorithms (specifically GRPO) in large-scale settings
Overview of the GSPO contribution: Stability, efficiency, and MoE compatibility

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Foundations of Policy Optimization Algorithms
outline.description: Before diving into GSPO, this chapter reviews the necessary theoretical background. It covers Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and its reliance on value models, then transitions to Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Students will learn how GRPO attempts to remove the value model by using group-relative advantages but retains token-level importance weighting, setting the stage for understanding where it fails.
subtopics: Review of PPO: Importance sampling, clipping, and the value model bottleneck
Deep dive into GRPO: Group-based advantage estimation without a value model
Mathematical formulation of token-level importance ratios in GRPO

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 3: Diagnosing Instability – Why Token-Level Weighting Fails
outline.description: This chapter provides a rigorous analysis of why GRPO suffers from instability. It explains the mathematical violation of importance sampling principles when applied to single-token samples within a sequence. The text details how high-variance noise accumulates over long sequences and interacts destructively with clipping mechanisms, leading to catastrophic failures specifically in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures.
subtopics: Theoretical requirements for valid importance sampling vs. token-level application
Analysis of high-variance noise accumulation in long-sequence generation
The interaction between clipping mechanisms and invalid weights
Expert-activation volatility in MoE models and its impact on token probabilities

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: The GSPO Algorithm – Core Principles and Formulation
outline.description: Here, the core innovation of GSPO is introduced. The chapter explains the shift from token-level to sequence-level optimization. Key concepts include defining importance ratios based on whole-sequence likelihood, applying length-normalization to stabilize values, and performing clipping at the sequence level. The mathematical derivation connects these choices back to the fundamental principles of matching the unit of reward with the unit of optimization.
subtopics: The principle of matching units: Sequence reward requires sequence optimization
Defining the sequence-level importance ratio $s_i(\theta)$ via geometric mean normalization
$L_1$ Normalization techniques for controlling numerical variance across lengths
$L_2$ Sequence-level clipping mechanics vs. token-level clipping
